messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nabil was a 22-year-old Middle Eastern man who had come to think of his life in terms of what might expose him. Before the assault, he had been a social, easygoing auditor, the kind of person who moved through client meetings with confidence and a dry sense of humor. The rape happened after a night out with someone he had been dating casually; he had trusted the relationship enough to be alone with the person, and what began as familiarity turned suddenly coercive and violent. In the months that followed, the smallest reminders could yank him back into the experience. A smell that resembled the room where it happened could make his stomach drop and send him hurrying away before he could think. If someone mentioned “my ex” in conversation, he would go rigid, hearing the phrase as if it were directed at him. When he encountered people behaving crudely, dismissively, or violating boundaries, it stirred the same sick sense of moral outrage and danger, as though the world had become full of people capable of what happened to him. Those moments did not just frighten him; they sharpened the judgment he had turned on himself. He had come to believe that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, that he should have seen it coming, and that he was permanently humiliated by what happened. He grieved the version of himself he felt he had lost, saying quietly that he used to be a happy person but now he was always miserable.

As the weeks went on, Nabil organized his life around staying one step ahead of anything that might unsettle him. He made sure to sit close to exits in restaurants, on the train, and in conference rooms at work, because being near a door gave him the feeling that he could escape before anything got worse. He began wearing concealing clothing, not because it fit his style, but because he did not want to be noticed or evaluated; the idea of other people judging his appearance or his performance felt unbearable, as if scrutiny might reveal the shame he believed was written on him. At work as an auditor, where he was expected to sit under the gaze of supervisors and clients, every review of his spreadsheets or presentation felt like a test of whether he still looked competent. He noticed that the more he hid himself and arranged the room for safety, the more convinced he became that he could not trust his own judgment. If he could not assess the danger in unfamiliar places, he reasoned, then he had to avoid them; he turned down new restaurants, new routes, and invitations to unfamiliar parts of the city. The strange part, to him, was that the more carefully he tried to control exposure, the more fragile he felt, and the more certain he became that danger was always waiting just beyond what he could manage.

That sense of vulnerability became especially intense around sudden movements from other people, which put him immediately on guard. A coworker reaching across the table too quickly, someone brushing past him in a hallway, even a door swinging open without warning would make his body tense and ready to react before his mind had caught up. Because he spent so much time scanning exits, faces, and hands, he was constantly primed for threat, and that hypervigilance made ordinary places feel potentially unsafe. He started noticing smells, gestures, and half-phrases everywhere, and the very acts of trying to avoid being caught off guard seemed to keep the assault alive in his mind. He had begun to associate people’s misbehavior, sudden motion, and even innocent references to relationships with what happened to him, and the more he arranged his days to prevent being noticed or trapped, the more his world seemed to confirm that he needed protection from it. His avoidance also fed the self-criticism he already carried: because he was never fully at ease, he interpreted his caution as proof that he was weaker than other people, and that only deepened his humiliation. In turn, those harsh conclusions made him more determined to hide, remain near exits, and avoid situations where anyone might evaluate him, which kept him from gathering experiences that might have challenged his fear.

By the time he sought help, Nabil was exhausted by the effort of keeping himself contained. He still went to work, but he arrived early to choose where he could sit, and he left as soon as he reasonably could. He described feeling constantly tense, as if his body had forgotten how to stand down. What brought him to treatment was the fear that his life was shrinking around the assault: he was tired of steering around smells, rooms, people, and places, and tired of feeling permanently marked by shame. He wanted relief from the belief that he had been ruined by what happened, though what frightened him most was the possibility that the misery, vigilance, and humiliation would simply become the rest of his life.
